Enthronement
en-THRONE-ment
noun
From the prefix en- (“to place in or on”) + throne (from Greek thronos, “seat of authority, royal chair”) + the suffix -ment (denoting the act or result of an action). The compound denotes the formal seating of a sovereign on the throne of authority — the investiture with all rights and powers of rule.

Biblical Definition

The enthronement of Christ is not a future expectation but a present and accomplished reality. The Psalter anticipates it: “Yet I have set My King on My holy hill of Zion” (Ps 2:6) — the divine decree by which the Father establishes the Messianic King against the rage of the nations. Psalm 110:1 discloses the act with unrivalled clarity: “The LORD said to my Lord, 'Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool'” — the text the New Testament cites more than any other Old Testament passage. The ascension accomplished what the cross and resurrection purchased: the exalted Christ was “seated at His right hand in the heavenly places” (Eph 1:20), far above every principality and power. John's Revelation opens its heavenly vision with a throne and One seated upon it (Rev 4:2) — the narrative axis around which the entire Apocalypse revolves. The enthronement is not static ceremony; it is the active government of the mediatorial Kingdom. Christ reigns now over history, over His church, and over His enemies — interceding for His people, subduing His foes through Word and Spirit, and advancing His kingdom until every knee bows. Reformed theology insists, against amillennial thinning and dispensationalist deferral alike, that the Lamb's enthronement is current and cosmic. The session at the Father's right hand is not a waiting posture but a ruling one — and the present age is the age of Christ's mediatorial reign.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster defines enthrone as the act of placing on a throne; to seat in a royal chair and invest with sovereign authority. Enthronement is the event and ceremony of that investiture.

expand to see more

ENTHRONE, v.t. [en and throne.] To place on a throne; to seat on a royal seat; to invest with sovereign authority and power. ENTHRONEMENT, n. The act of placing on a throne; the ceremony of investing with royal power and dignity; the formal beginning of a reign.

Applied to the Lord Jesus Christ, enthronement denotes His exaltation to the right hand of the Father following His ascension — the moment at which His mediatorial kingship, earned by His obedience and ratified by His resurrection, was formally and publicly established over heaven and earth.

Key Scripture

Ps 2:6 — "“Yet I have set My King on My holy hill of Zion.”"

Ps 110:1 — "The LORD said to my Lord, “Sit at My right hand, till I make Your enemies Your footstool.”"

Eph 1:20 — "which He brought about in Christ — when He raised Him from the dead, and seated Him at His right hand in the heavenly places,"

Rev 4:2 — "Immediately I was in the Spirit — and behold, a throne stood in heaven, and One sitting on the throne."

Modern Corruption

Liberal theology domesticates the enthronement into a symbol of spiritual influence; dispensationalism defers the Davidic throne to a future millennium, effectively denying that Christ is presently reigning as King.

expand to see more

Two distortions recur in the church's handling of Christ's enthronement. The first is liberal domestication: the session at the Father's right hand is reduced to a metaphor for Christ's spiritual presence or moral example, stripped of its regal, governmental, and judicial content. The second is dispensational deferral: Christ's Davidic kingship is projected entirely into a future millennial era, so that He does not yet occupy His appointed throne. Both errors share a common defect — they refuse to read Psalm 110:1 as the New Testament itself reads it: as a present and ongoing reality entered at the ascension.

Confessional Reformed theology holds, with the Westminster Larger Catechism (QQ. 45, 54) and the 1689 London Baptist Confession (ch. 8), that Christ entered His kingly office fully at His exaltation. He is not king-elect awaiting inauguration but the reigning Mediator whose rule is executed now through Word and Spirit. The enthronement secures the church's confidence: her Lord is not absent but governing, and every present affliction unfolds under the superintendence of the One who holds all authority in heaven and earth.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From the Greek thronos (“royal seat”) and the biblical imagery of the right-hand seat of authority — the highest place of honor and governmental power in the ancient world, applied to Christ's present mediatorial reign.

expand to see more

Greek thronos — seat of authority, royal chair; used of God's heavenly throne in Isaiah and Revelation

Hebrew kissē' — throne, seat of royal authority; used of God's cosmic throne and David's earthly type

Psalm 110:1 — the most-cited Old Testament text in the New Testament; the foundational warrant for Christ's present session

Latin sessio — a sitting; the technical Reformed-scholastic term for Christ's post-ascension mediatorial reign

Ephesians 1:20–23 — the apostolic proclamation of Christ's exaltation above every name and power

Usage

"The enthronement of Christ answers every accusation that the gospel has failed: the King is not absent but ruling, advancing His kingdom through the preaching of the Word and the conversion of the nations."

"Christian doxology is shaped by the enthronement: every Lord's Day service, every psalm of praise, is offered to the ascended and reigning Lord — not to a Christ still in the manger or still on the cross."

"Revelation's throne-room vision (chs. 4–5) interprets earthly suffering through the lens of the enthronement: whatever the beast may attempt, the Lamb is on the throne."
